 Social Security chief identifies 'first solution' as program faces funding concerns
 Frank Bisignano said the agency has reviewed 100% of its database, correcting records with missing death dates and citizenship information

 Twitter 
 Threads 
 Print 
 Email 
 Add Fox Business on Google 
 By Arabella Bennett FOXBusiness close video Social Security chief details historic records cleanup, solvency warnings 
 Social Security Administration Commissioner Frank Bisignano discusses the historic cleanup of nearly 50 million files, warnings over program solvency and new Trump Account notices sent to eligible families.
 Social Security Administration Commissioner Frank Bisignano said "eliminating fraud, waste and abuse" is the "first solution" to protecting the retirement program as concerns persist over its long-term finances.
 During an appearance on "Big Money in the Morning," Bisignano discussed efforts to improve agency records, modernize operations and safeguard the program.
 "The president has been very, very clear. Protect and preserve. The first steps of protecting was to get the operations to work right. Any good business fixes its technology, fixes its operations, fixes its books and records, and that's what's been going on," Bisignano said.
 Social Security Commissioner Frank Bisignano says eliminating fraud, waste and abuse is the first step toward preserving the program. (Tierney L. Cross / Getty Images) 
 The comments come as Social Security faces a longstanding funding challenge. The program relies primarily on payroll taxes to pay benefits, while its trust funds help cover the difference when costs exceed incoming revenue. 
 Without legislative changes, depletion of those reserves would not mean benefits would stop altogether, but incoming taxes alone would be insufficient to pay scheduled benefits in full.
 SOCIAL SECURITY CORRECTS NEARLY 50 MILLION RECORDS IN LARGEST SSN CLEANUP IN AGENCY HISTORY 
 close video Senator Bill Cassidy discusses proposed $1.5T Social Security investment fund 
 Louisiana Senator Bill Cassidy discusses his proposed $1.5 trillion investment fund to address Social Security shortfalls, while Bill Sweeney from AARP reacts to the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment.
 The agency has also been working to correct incomplete or inaccurate records, including missing dates of death and citizenship information. 
 HOW CONGRESS COULD ADDRESS SOCIAL SECURITY INSOLVENCY – AND THE HIDDEN COST 
 Bisignano said the cleanup involves the agency’s entire database, clarifying that the roughly 15% figure discussed in the interview referred to records corrected, not the share reviewed.
 President Donald Trump and Social Security Commissioner Frank Bisignano are prioritizing efforts to protect and preserve Social Security for future generations. (Anna Moneymaker / Getty Images) 
 "15% is the amount of records that were corrected. We've gone through 100%," he said.
 Bisignano also described artificial intelligence as a tool for improving service, processing and recordkeeping, while emphasizing coordination between government agencies.
